Photograph: Rockstar Opinion Games We made GTA 6, the world’s biggest video game – we should have working conditions to match Nestor Uriarte After the release of Grand Theft Auto VI this week, Rockstar employees like me can make history again. We need union recognition to safeguard our jobs Wed 18 Nov 2026 06.50 EST Last modified on Wed 18 Nov 2026 07.27 EST Share W hen I first got the call offering me a job at Rockstar, I was thrilled. I thought back to being a child and sneaking into my brother’s room to grab the PlayStation Portable so I could secretly play Grand Theft Auto: Vice City Stories. The same kid who fell in love with Rockstar’s games back then now gets to spend every day helping to create those worlds as an animation programmer at the studio in Edinburgh. This week, we will celebrate the culmination of more than a decade of effort: the release of the most anticipated game of all time, Grand Theft Auto VI . But our team has the opportunity to make history a second time this month. Right now, the ballot is open for Rockstar employees to decide whether we want the union we have built with our colleagues to get recognition. As someone who cares deeply about our team, cares about what we do, and wants us to be able to keep delivering world-class games into the future, I’m voting yes.

It’s called Earth Overshoot Day . In 1971, it fell on Dec. 25. Disturbingly, by 2022, it fell on July 28. In short, we humans need 1.75 Earths to support our current rate of consumption! That is unsustainable, and we have to make changes. So, how can we slow down our current consumption rate, while ensuring equitable progress and resources for all? pages.text: We Sent a Cartographer to the Sale of One of America's Most Famous Maps | National Geographic By Nina Strochlic Published October 29, 2026 1:09 On a spring day in 1982, a never-before-sold piece went under the hammer at Christie's auction house in New York City. In a moment he later said left him breathless, Malcolm Forbes, Jr., the president of Forbes magazine, raised his paddle and won the hand-drawn survey of the Mason-Dixon Line for $360,000—the most ever spent on an American map at the time. The sale shocked bidders: As the price climbed to more than 20 times its estimated sale price, it also managed to overshadow a rare copy of the Declaration of Independence (which fetched $285,000). The losing bidder for the Mason-Dixon map was the Library of Congress. Forbes ended up with an unusual-looking relic: six sheets of paper conjoined into a manuscript just six and a half inches tall and over six feet long. It’s believed to be the only original copy of the western section of the Mason Dixon survey—the most famous border in America. ( Why Your Mental Map of the World Is (Probably) Wrong .) More than 40 years later, that same map has now sold for $1,187,500 to an anonymous buyer, according to Brunk Auctions in North Carolina. The bidding started at $400,000, a sale price that doubled within mere minutes. Today, the Mason-Dixon Line is synonymous with a divided America, and its darkest era. Coastal areas typically have mild weather, while the interior has greater seasonal variation in temperature and precipitation. In Nome, yearly precipitation averages about 15 inches, and the average temperature is about 21 o F. Summers average around 50 o F. The first snow dusting of the year can fall as early as August, although heavy snowfall begins in October and will stay on the ground until May. Winter temperatures typically range from -10 to -20 o F, although it can reach as low as -65 o F, with an even lower windchill factor. With these extreme temperatures, the sea ice in the Bering and Chukchi Sea will freeze up around mid-October and remain frozen until breakup in late-May. Photograph: Fadel Senna/AFP/Getty Images Weather tracker Environment This article is more than 7 months old Analysis Weather tracker: Thunderstorms drench UAE and Saudi Arabia This article is more than 7 months old James Michelin for MetDesk Abnormally strong jet stream triggers deluge in Middle East, while north Africa braces for 60-80mph gusts Mon 30 Mar 2026 10.31 BST Last modified on Tue 31 Mar 2026 05.09 BST Share An unusual weather pattern unleashed severe thunderstorms across parts of the Middle East last week, battering countries including the United Arab Emirates and Saudi Arabia. The Arabian peninsula – typically dominated by arid desert climates – received up to 150mm of rain in just a few days. The deluge was caused by an abnormally strong jet stream, which helped a deep area of low pressure to develop north of Saudi Arabia . This, in turn, drew moist tropical air from the Indian Ocean and triggered intense storms. In Oman, hailstones as large as tennis balls fell during Wednesday evening’s storms, alongside torrential rain. Doha, Qatar’s capital, experienced flooding the same day. Weatherization Assistance Program The U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) Weatherization Assistance Program (WAP) reduces energy costs for low-income households by increasing the energy efficiency of their homes, while ensuring their health and safety. The program supports 8,500 jobs and provides weatherization services to approximately 32,000 homes every year using DOE funds. Web Policies Accessibility The U.S. Department of Energy is committed to providing access to our web pages for individuals with disabilities. To meet this commitment, this site is built to comply with the requirements of Section 508 of the Rehabilitation Act . Section 508 requires that individuals with disabilities, who are members of the public seeking information or services from us, have access to and use of information and data that is comparable to that provided to the public who are not individuals with disabilities, unless an undue burden would be imposed on us. Section 508 also requires us to ensure that Federal employees with disabilities have access to and use of information and data that is comparable to the access to and use of information and data by Federal employees who are not individuals with disabilities, unless an undue burden would be imposed on us. Search Twitter YouTube Facebook Instagram Flickr LinkedIn Weeds and Invasives The BLM manages 245 million acres of public lands primarily in the Western United States, including Alaska. Seventy-nine million of these acres are impacted by noxious and invasive weeds. One of the BLM's highest priorities is to promote ecosystem health and one of the greatest obstacles to achieving this goal is the rapid expansion of weeds across public lands. These invasive plants can dominate and often cause permanent damage to natural plant communities. If not eradicated or controlled, noxious weeds will continue to jeopardize the health of the public lands and to constrain the myriad activities that occur on public lands. About Weeds and Invasives The term "weed" means different things to different people. In the broadest sense, it is any plant growing where it is not wanted. Weeds can be native or non-native, invasive or non invasive, and noxious or not noxious. Learn more and review Frequently Asked Questions . Set yourself up for success If you're like many people with prediabetes or type 2 diabetes, weight loss is part of your treatment plan. It sounds so simple: eat less and move more. But if weight loss were that easy, millions of people wouldn't be struggling right now to do it. And you've probably noticed that even people who take the weight off have a hard time keeping it off. More and more studies show that people respond differently to diets. For example, some lose weight on low carb; some gain weight. The same goes for other plans. This excerpt from the Baseball Traveler newsletter, presented by Circle K, is a mere taste of the smorgasbord of delights he offers every week. Read the full newsletter here , and subscribe to his newsletter here . They took the field in those jerseys?! No corner of the sports world has prompted this incredulous query more than Minor League Baseball, whose teams regularly wear outlandish theme jerseys in addition to their regular uniforms. To be a Minor League fan is to be exposed, on a daily basis, to a cornucopia of bold colors and bolder design. Check out jerseys in the MiLB Shop Ten examples of some of the boldest –- and probably the weirdest -- can be found below, all of which debuted during the era of sartorial excess that was the 2010s. Let's take a trip down memory lane, marveling anew at these groundbreaking and bizarre Minor League jerseys. (Note: Teams are listed at their current affiliation and level of play, which may have changed since the time these jerseys were first worn.) Bacon-themed uniforms (Lehigh Valley IronPigs, Triple-A PHI, 2014) Like Dylan going electric in 1965, the IronPigs' bacon-themed duds were an epochal event that firmly delineated the start of a new era. These uniforms, featuring bacon-strip hats and jerseys with a strip of bacon underneath a "'Pigs" wordmark, planted the seed for the food-themed alternate identity craze that continues in the Minor Leagues to this day. Feel the sizzle. Organ Donor

At the U.S. Department of Labor's Office of Disability Employment Policy (ODEP), we work to increase success for people with disabilities in America's workplaces. This is a goal we share with our Alliance partner the Professional Baseball Athletic Trainers Society (PBATS). Over the years, ODEP and PBATS have collaborated on a number of activities, including the production of several public service announcements (PSAs) featuring former MLB players with disabilities and/or professional baseball athletic trainers from clubs around the country. Among the topics these PSAs address is the importance of helping people stay at or return to work after injury or illness and, most recently, strategies for fostering mental health-friendly workplaces. Please view and share these PSAs and explore our resources for fostering supportive workplaces, for all workers in all types of workplaces—because everyone should be in the game. Wellbore Construction and Evaluation Wellbores are a critical component of the infrastructure and success of geothermal electricity generation projects and represent a significant hurdle for developers. Improving the durability and costs of wellbore structures and ensuring long-term well flow are vital to reduce costs and ensure safe, efficient operation of geothermal power plants. The Office of Geothermal is funding projects that can support these needs for both next-generation and conventional geothermal systems. By improving ways to build, assess, and maintain geothermal wellbores, these projects will expand opportunities to tap firm, flexible, domestic geothermal energy nationwide. Wells of Opportunity A key step to unlocking the full potential of reliable, domestic geothermal energy may lie inside millions of American oil and gas wells . These wells can be used to harness geothermal energy in two ways: through the retrofitting of inactive or unproductive wells, or through co-production on active wells. Well Retrofits In well retrofits, an unused, dry, or unproductive oil and gas well first undergoes any repairs necessary for safe operation. Water is then pumped into the oil and gas well, where it is warmed by the earth and drawn back to the surface to power a thermoelectric generator. The hot water pulled to the surface can be used for heating, cooling, or to power nearby structures and homes. America has millions of dry or unproductive oil and gas wells, many of which could be retrofitted for geothermal use. Note: The scope of the Office of Geothermal’s WOO initiative specifically targets inactive or unproductive wells. Wendin Smith Wendin Smith Dr. Wendin D. Smith currently serves as the National Nuclear Security Administration (NNSA) Associate Administrator and Deputy Under Secretary for Counterterrorism and Counterproliferation. In this position, Dr. Smith is responsible for overseeing and advancing programs that counter nuclear terrorism and nuclear proliferation. Dr. Smith's organization also manages capabilities to prepare for and respond to nuclear and radiological accidents and incidents worldwide. Dr. Smith recently served as Director of Security Policy at the North Atlantic Treaty Organization’s (NATO) Headquarters in Brussels, Belgium. In this capacity, she coordinated the division’s work related to multilateral organizations, NATO affairs and security policy, as well as arms control, disarmament, and nonproliferation. Previously, she was Managing Director with Deloitte Consulting, LLC. In prior roles with the Department of Defense, she served as the Senior Advisor to the U.S. Special Operations Command for Countering Weapons of Mass Destruction (CWMD), and as the Deputy Assistant Secretary of Defense for CWMD. Reconstruction of a Neanderthal man (Homo neanderthalensis), based on the La Chapelle-aux-Saints fossils. Researchers think that prehistoric interbreeding between Neanderthals and Homo sapiens was most likely skewed toward male Neanderthals with female modern humans . S. Entressangle/E. Daynes/Science Photo Library By Annie Roth Published February 26, 2026 Neanderthal men may have had a thing for modern human women, or perhaps Neanderthal men had something human women couldn't resist. That’s one potential interpretation of a new study, published Thursday in Science , that found when Neanderthals and Homo sapiens interbred, the pairings were predominantly between Neanderthal men and human women. Scientists have long known that some of our ancestors reproduced with Neanderthals before the species went extinct roughly 40,000 years ago. Today, traces of Neanderthal DNA linger in the genomes of many people, particularly among those with non-African ancestry. On average, it amounts to about one to two percent of a person’s genome. However, these leftover bits of DNA aren't evenly distributed throughout the genome. pages.text: We’ve Been Strapping Cargo to Our Backs for Millions of Years, but Backpack Innovation Really Took Off Around the Civil War Skip to main content Illustration by Emily Lankiewicz / Images via public domain Humans have been carting things on our backs in wraps of some kind at least since we began using tools, around two million years ago—and we have always sought ways to make the load more comfortable. The oldest known backpack ever discovered, in the Alps on the border between Austria and Italy, employed two narrow wooden boards and a hazel rod for a frame. The contraption dates to around 3300 B.C. and is credited to Ötzi the Iceman , a glacier mummy unearthed alongside it in 1991. But what we recognize as a backpack is much newer. In 1865, Henry Clay Merriam led a regiment of Black Union troops in an attack against Fort Blakely, a Confederate stronghold in Alabama. His deeds in this final battle of the Civil War earned him a Medal of Honor “for conspicuous gallantry.” Afterward, the lieutenant colonel had an epiphany: It was burdensome to carry both a knapsack (a pack with shoulder straps but no frame for internal support) and a haversack (a shoulder bag containing his rations). Based on his time carrying gear for the Army, Merriam devised a solution: a boxy canvas pack with room for socks, a quart of water, a shaving kit and a deck of cards, plus a compartment for rations in a case at the bottom.
